rows.name: Arrow-key steering sprite

rows.name: Phonics revision – level 6
steps: Revise long vowel patterns: i saying /igh/, o saying /u/, ey saying /ee/.

rows.name: Missing Number Mystery Cards
rows.unit: Addition and Subtraction of Whole Numbers
steps: Give each pair 10 cards, each showing an equation with one box hidden, such as 4,350 + __ = 6,000 or __ - 2,478 = 1,300.

rows.name: Certain, Likely, Unlikely, Impossible Bag Game
steps: Show four labels on the board: certain, likely, unlikely, impossible.

levels.2: A photograph is taken and the child says what they chose to show and why.

rows.note: event named in the cell; steps and levels built from the event name and common sense; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Celebration of Learning – BharatQuest (Journey Through India's Legacy)
steps: Each group picks one place, person or tradition from India's heritage already met in class.
Groups prepare a two-minute quest stop (a talk, poster or short act).
Other children visit each stop as a quest.
At the end, each child names one thing they learned.
rows.materials: poster paper, markers

levels.0: The stop is not prepared or has no content about India's heritage.
levels.1: The stop is presented only with heavy prompting or reading directly from notes.
levels.2: One piece of India's heritage is shared clearly with at least one correct fact.
levels.3: The heritage piece is shared and compared with another place or tradition.

rows.note: event named in the cell; steps and levels built from the event name and common sense; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Evaluation – 1
steps: Explain what the evaluation covers and how long it takes.
Children complete the evaluation task quietly on their own.
Educator collects the work and notes areas to revisit.
Hold a short reflection circle on what felt easy and what felt hard.
rows.materials: evaluation paper

levels.0: The evaluation is left mostly blank.
levels.1: Parts of the evaluation are completed only with repeated prompts or reading help.
levels.2: The evaluation is completed within the given time without help.
levels.3: The evaluation is completed and the child explains one mistake and how to fix it.

rows.note: event named in the cell; steps and levels built from the event name and common sense; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Dribbling, passing and coordination
steps: Warm up with running and jumping.
Set out a line of cones.
Each child dribbles the football around the cones, then passes to a partner.
Partners pass back and forth while moving.
Cool down with stretches.
rows.materials: footballs, cones

levels.0: The ball runs away from the feet at nearly every touch.
levels.1: The ball is dribbled around cones only while moving slowly or after a demonstration.
levels.2: The ball stays close to the feet around all the cones at a steady pace.
levels.3: The ball is dribbled around cones and passed accurately to a moving partner.

rows.note: session named in the cell; steps and levels built from the event name and common sense; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Dodgeball and functional training
steps: Warm up with hopping drills.
Explain the dodgeball rules.
Play rounds of dodgeball in two teams.
Finish with strength exercises such as squats and planks, each held for a short count.
rows.materials: soft balls, open space

levels.0: Is hit repeatedly without moving, or throws leave the play area.
levels.1: Throws and dodges follow the rules only with the educator calling the rules.
levels.2: Balls are thrown at legal targets and dodged while following the rules.
levels.3: The throws and dodges follow the rules and the child helps a team-mate plan a play.

rows.note: session named in the cell; steps and levels built from the event name and common sense; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Football, athletics and speed training
steps: Warm up with jogging.
Practise basic defending and goalkeeping in pairs.
Run sprints over a marked distance.
Run an endurance lap at a steady pace.
Cool down with stretches.
rows.materials: football, cones, open ground

levels.0: The sprint has a stumbling start or the child stops before the line.
levels.1: A set distance is sprinted only when a partner runs alongside.
levels.2: A set distance is sprinted with a steady start and finish.
levels.3: The sprint is steady and the child compares times across two attempts and explains the change.

rows.note: session named in the cell; steps and levels built from the event name and common sense; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: Teamwork and strategy – Lagori introduction
steps: Explain how Lagori is played.
Split into two teams.
Each team discusses a plan before each round.
Play rounds and talk about what worked.
rows.materials: seven flat stones, a soft ball

levels.0: The team does not discuss, or the plan is ignored during play.
levels.1: A move is chosen only when the educator suggests one.
levels.2: A move is chosen by the team and the child gives a reason for it.
levels.3: The move is chosen, explained, and changed after the round with a reason.

rows.note: session named in the cell; steps and levels built from the event name and common sense; no educator plan exists; steps are suggested: made up from the activity name and unit, not from a plan

rows.name: B1 The Cornerstone maze – shorten the route with repeat
steps: Tape a grid on the floor and place obstacles; one child is the robot. The only instructions are forward, turn left, turn right.
Write the algorithm that gets the robot from start to finish (Worksheet 5) and walk it out.
Find the instructions that repeat and rewrite the route using REPEAT n TIMES (Worksheet 7).
Count the instructions in the long and the looped version and write how many were saved.
Explain to a Grade 2 child what REPEAT means and write what you said.
Write one reason you would keep the long version.
rows.materials: floor tape, obstacles, Worksheets 5 and 7
rows.note: Grade 4 job in the shared Cornerstone maze project; the display shows the saving, e.g. 19 instructions became 7.

levels.0: Worksheet 5 is left blank or lists moves with no turns, so a robot classmate cannot reach the finish.
levels.1: Only with a partner calling out each move at the taped grid does a full forward and turn route appear on paper.
levels.2: A complete list of forward, turn left and turn right steps on Worksheet 5 walks the robot from start to finish around every obstacle.
levels.3: Given a fresh obstacle layout, a new route is written unaided, and the reason for keeping the long version is that each step stays easy to check.

rows.name: B2 Catch the food – falling objects with repetition
steps: Choose a theme the school is already studying and storyboard a game where a sprite catches falling objects.
Write the paper algorithm first, then build it in Scratch.
Use repetition so the objects keep falling without repeated blocks.
Add one rule for what happens when you miss.
Swap with a partner to play and debug each other's game.
rows.materials: Scratch, storyboard paper
rows.note: Grade 4 job: repetition and a miss rule; display uses a QR code beside the storyboard.

levels.0: Objects fall once and stop, or the Scratch script shows the same block pasted many times with no loop.
levels.1: Following a partner's pointer to the forever block, the catcher game finally keeps objects falling.
levels.2: Food keeps dropping from the top of the Scratch stage inside one repeat or forever block, with no copied blocks.
levels.3: Swapped to a partner's game, a bug in the repeat count is spotted and fixed by changing the number or the loop type.

rows.name: B3 What our class is like – survey, chart and two sentences
steps: Choose a question worth asking, such as how we get to school, what is in our tiffin or how many minutes we read.
Write what you think the answer will be (Worksheet 8) and collect the data across the school.
Enter the data on the computer.
Make the chart on the computer, sketching it on paper first.
Write two sentences about what the chart shows that a tally could not.
Say whether you were right and what surprised you.
rows.materials: Worksheet 8, computer with spreadsheet
rows.note: Grade 4 job: chart it and write two sentences.

levels.0: No survey question is chosen, or the tally sheet holds only the answers of two or three neighbours.
levels.1: Using a ready-made question from the educator's list, responses are gathered across the school but several entries are missing a category.
levels.2: Responses from children across the school are gathered on Worksheet 8 and typed into the spreadsheet, one row per answer.
levels.3: Asked a new question such as minutes read, a fresh class tally is planned and collected with its categories chosen in advance.

rows.name: B4 How a message travels – children become the network
steps: Choose one sender, one receiver and several routers; the message is a folded paper.
Break the message into packets and send them by different routes.
Cut a router out mid-delivery and see what happens.
Say what happens when a route fails and why more than one path is safer.
rows.materials: folded paper messages, string and cards
rows.note: Grade 4 job: what happens when a route fails.

levels.0: The cards for sender, receiver and routers stay unlabelled and no device is named aloud.
levels.1: When the card key shows sender, router and receiver, each device is named as the string is passed along.
levels.2: Sender, receiver and each router are named aloud by their cards as the folded message goes from hand to hand.
levels.3: In a rearranged network with extra routers, every device is named and a second path is shown when one router is cut out.

rows.name: B5 Animate a story – one scene with a loop and a second algorithm
steps: Take a story the class already knows (for example the greedy dog or a Hindi folk tale) and choose one scene.
Storyboard the scene on paper, then write the algorithm, then the code.
Use a loop for anything that repeats.
Add a second algorithm running at the same time.
Display the storyboard beside a printed strip of screenshots.
rows.materials: Scratch, storyboard paper
rows.note: Grade 4 job: loops and a parallel algorithm.

levels.0: The Scratch sprite stays still on the stage and the storyboard has one frame only.
levels.1: Pointing from the storyboard strip, a partner helps build the move blocks, and the sprite glides in just one direction.
levels.2: A sprite in the chosen scene glides or walks across the stage as the code runs, matching the storyboard panels.
levels.3: Beside the printed screenshot strip, the sprite is shown moving in a second scene of a new story, with one panel explained aloud.

rows.name: B6 Build something that senses – input, process, output
steps: Choose a micro:bit or similar device that reacts to light, movement or a button, or build a mechanical machine such as a lever, a pulley or a marble run.
Label the input, the process and the output on the machine.
Write the algorithm the machine follows.
Make the machine repeat without being reset.
Show it with three labelled arrows and a "press here" sign.
rows.materials: micro:bit or recycled and mechanical materials
rows.note: Grade 4 job: make it repeat without being reset.

levels.0: Neither the machine nor its arrows have labels, so input, process and output cannot be told apart.
levels.1: With a three-box label template and a reminder card, the micro:bit or lever machine is labelled but the process arrow points the wrong way.
levels.2: Three labelled arrows on the machine mark the light, button or push as input, the rule it follows as process, and the sound, light or motion as output.
levels.3: Explaining another group's marble run to a visitor, the input, process and output are picked out and a misplaced label is moved.

rows.name: The Broken Robot Artist – drawing a square with precise commands
steps: The educator is a drawing robot who only does what is said, exactly; the class calls out instructions to draw a square.
Vague instructions ("draw a line", "turn") fail; ask for exact distances and a 90-degree turn.
Grade 4 students draw a flowchart: Start, Move 100, Turn 90, Move 100, Turn 90, repeating.
Add the Pen extension in Scratch; build the long-hand code: Erase All, Pen Down, then four pairs of Move 100 and Turn Right 90.
Test what happens with 91 degrees by mistake.
Worksheet: translate a text recipe for a triangle (move 150, turn right 120, three times) into a block stack.
rows.materials: whiteboard, Scratch with Pen extension, Grade 4 worksheet
rows.note: Replaces the shorter planner summary of the same session.

levels.0: Calls like draw a line or turn are left vague, so the robot educator stays frozen at the board.
levels.1: Prompted by the educator-robot's refusal, the instructions gain a distance but the 90-degree turn stays missing.
levels.2: Flowchart boxes read Start, Move 100, Turn 90, Move 100, Turn 90 with exact numbers, and the Scratch stack draws a closed square.
levels.3: A triangle recipe of move 150 and turn right 120 three times becomes a working block stack, and a slip such as 91 degrees is explained as a gap in the figure.

rows.name: No Technology Challenge and the story of Aro
steps: Show pictures of a mobile, pizza, a house and fire and ask "What if all these disappeared today? How would you survive?"; children brainstorm.
Tell the story of Aro, a boy who wakes in a cave with no school, electricity, supermarkets or phones and must find food before sunset and stay safe from wild animals.
Ask: What problems would Aro face? Where would he sleep? How would he eat?
Discuss food, shelter, clothing and protection with pictures.
Close by completing: "I think the hardest part of being an early human was…"
rows.materials: pictures of caves, stone tools, animal cards, chart paper

source.cell: Session 1 – Who Were the Early Humans? (starter, introduction, plenary)

rows.note: Plan is Grades 2–4 shared; Big Question: "If you lived 20,000 years ago, how would you survive?"

levels.0: Questions about Aro's problems get no answer, or the plenary sentence stays unfinished.
levels.1: Looking at the cave, tool and animal pictures, one need such as food or shelter is named after a prompt.
levels.2: Aro's food, shelter, clothing and protection are each described aloud, and the sentence about the hardest part is finished.
levels.3: Asked what Aro would do if the cave flooded, an answer about moving to higher ground or keeping a fire is given with a reason.

rows.name: Survival Stations
steps: Set up four classroom stations.
Station 1 Food sorting: sort food into edible and not edible.
Station 2 Build a cave with blocks or paper.
Station 3 Stone Tool Detective: match each tool to its purpose (hunting, cutting, digging).
Station 4 Animal Danger: sort animals into friendly and dangerous.
Exit ticket: circle how early humans protected themselves (fire, television, cars, computers).
rows.materials: blocks or paper, stone tool images or replicas, animal picture cards

levels.0: Station cards go unsorted, and the exit ticket circle is blank or lands on television or computers.
levels.1: Beside a partner who reads the picture cards, tools and animals are sorted but the cave station stays unbuilt.
levels.2: Food is sorted into edible and not edible, tools are matched to hunting, cutting or digging, and fire is circled on the exit ticket.
levels.3: Faced with a new card such as a bone needle, a use is guessed from its shape and linked to how early humans protected themselves.

rows.name: Become Archaeologists
steps: Bury stone tool pictures, animal cards and paper bones in a sand tray.
Students dig and identify the artifacts they find.
Say what each artifact was used for.
rows.materials: sand tray, stone tool pictures, animal cards, paper bones

levels.0: Pictures dug from the sand tray are set aside unnamed with no use given.
levels.1: Using the tool-and-purpose key card, artefacts from the tray are named but each use is read out from the card.
levels.2: Each dug-up stone tool, animal card or paper bone is named, and a use such as cutting meat or digging roots is said.
levels.3: A mystery object buried by a classmate is identified and its use is argued from its shape and from matching tools.

rows.name: Cave Art Gallery
steps: Talk about why early humans made cave paintings: to tell stories, record animals and teach others; show famous cave painting images.
On brown chart paper, draw hunting scenes, animals, handprints and a campfire.
Use only brown, black, red and yellow.
Display the gallery and say what each painting tells.
rows.materials: brown craft paper, chalk, charcoal pencils

levels.0: The gallery paintings have no explanation, and no reason is given for early people painting.
levels.1: Guided by the display of famous cave paintings, one purpose such as telling stories is repeated for the painted hunting scene.
levels.2: A painted campfire or tool on the brown paper is explained as telling others how fire gave warmth or stone tools helped hunting.
levels.3: Standing at the gallery, a visitor hears why a handprint or a hunting scene shows what fire and tools changed in daily life.

rows.name: Mystery Box and Timeline Race
steps: Mystery box holds a stone, a stick, a leaf and a torch; ask which one changed human history the most.
Discuss the benefits of fire (cooking, warmth, protection, light) and what stone tools did (hunting, cutting, digging).
Timeline Race: arrange stone tools, then fire, then cave paintings, then farming.
Plenary: say which discovery was most important and explain why.
rows.materials: mystery box, timeline cards

source.cell: Session 2 – Starter, Teaching and Activity 3: Timeline Race

levels.0: The torch, stone, stick or leaf is chosen at random with no reason.
levels.1: With the timeline cards in a given order and a sentence starter, the torch is picked and one benefit of fire is named.
levels.2: Fire is picked from the mystery box, and cooking, warmth, protection and light are given as reasons it changed human history.
levels.3: Ranking fire against stone tools in the plenary, a reason is argued that decides which discovery mattered most.

rows.name: Can You Survive? – inquiry project
steps: Groups receive an environment: forest, desert, snow or grassland.
Plan the shelter, food, clothing and safety they would need.
Present the survival plan to the class and use evidence to justify it.
rows.materials: chart paper, atlas or world map

source.cell: Final Cambridge Inquiry Project: "Can You Survive?"

levels.0: The environment card stays unused and the plan has no shelter, food, clothing or safety.
levels.1: Helped by the atlas and a group member's prompts, a plan for the forest covers shelter and food but misses clothing.
levels.2: Shelter, food, clothing and safety are each planned for the desert, snow or grassland and shown on the chart paper.
levels.3: Questioned by the class, the plan is defended with evidence such as why snow needs thick clothing and a fire.

rows.name: 3D Name Stand (Fortnight 1)
steps: Fold chart paper into a standing shape.
Write and decorate your name.
Add designs and patterns.
rows.materials: chart paper, scale, pencil, colours
rows.note: Objective: children create a standing paper name display.

levels.0: Chart paper is left flat and the name does not stand up.
levels.1: With an educator's pre-scored fold lines, the paper stands but the name leans or falls over.
levels.2: A folded chart paper name stand stays upright on the desk with the name written on the front face.
levels.3: Redesigning the stand with a wider base or a second fold, a taller version holds up for a friend's name too.

rows.name: Nature Texture Art (Fortnight 2)
steps: Place a leaf below the paper.
Rub a crayon gently.
Observe the texture impressions.
rows.materials: leaves, bark textures, crayons, paper

levels.0: No impression appears on the paper, or the leaf is not placed under it.
levels.1: Using a single leaf set by a partner, a crayon rubbing shows veins but the texture word is borrowed from the neighbour.
levels.2: Rubbing the crayon over the leaf and bark leaves clear vein and ridge marks, and each is labelled as rough, smooth, soft or hard.
levels.3: Choosing a new surface such as a coin, cloth or brick wall, a rubbing is made and its feel is described in a sentence.

rows.name: Animal Clay Sculptures (Fortnight 3)
steps: Watch the educator demonstrate joining clay parts.
Create an animal.
Add details and textures.
rows.materials: clay, sculpting sticks

levels.0: The clay stays in a lump or the parts fall apart.
levels.1: After the educator demonstration and a repeat of the joining steps, the legs stay attached only when the educator presses them.
levels.2: An animal with a body, head and legs joined firmly keeps its shape, and the sculpting stick adds fur or scales.
levels.3: Making a second animal from memory, pieces are joined without cracks and a different texture is added to each.

rows.name: Paper Weaving (Fortnight 4)
steps: Prepare slits in the base sheet.
Weave coloured paper strips over and under.
Secure the strips with glue.
rows.materials: coloured paper strips, base sheet, glue

levels.0: The base sheet has no slits cut or the strips lie side by side without crossing.
levels.1: Following the first row woven by a partner, the strips go over and under but the pattern is lost by the third row.
levels.2: Coloured strips pass over and under across every row of the slit sheet, and glue holds the ends.
levels.3: Swapping to strips of two widths, the weave is finished with a new alternating pattern and the sequence is explained.

rows.name: Recycled Material Organizer (Fortnight 5)
steps: Design the organizer.
Join the materials.
Paint and decorate it.
rows.materials: cardboard boxes, bottle caps, glue, paint

levels.0: Boxes and bottle caps remain a pile and no organizer is joined.
levels.1: Using a sketch drawn with the educator, a few parts are glued but the organizer wobbles without support.
levels.2: Cardboard boxes and bottle caps are joined into a standing organizer with compartments, then painted.
levels.3: Fitting desk items such as pens and rulers in, a compartment is resized or added to suit them.

rows.name: Block Printing (Fortnight 6)
steps: Dip the potato or sponge block in paint.
Press repeatedly.
Create print designs on cloth or paper.
rows.materials: potato or sponge blocks, paint, cloth or paper
rows.note: Explores repeated print patterns.

levels.0: One single print sits on the cloth, with no repeat.
levels.1: Marked with pencil dots to press on, the sponge prints repeat in a line but gaps and overlaps appear.
levels.2: The same potato or sponge block is pressed again and again, giving a repeated row of at least five prints.
levels.3: Alternating two blocks or two colours, a new repeating pattern is printed and its repeat unit is named.

rows.name: Pencil Holder Craft (Fortnight 7)
steps: Fix tissue rolls on a cardboard base.
Paint it creatively.
Decorate with patterns.
rows.materials: tissue rolls, cardboard base, paint
rows.note: Functional desk accessory.

levels.0: Tissue rolls lie loose beside the cardboard base, with nothing fixed.
levels.1: Held steady by an educator, the rolls are glued to the base yet one tips over when a pencil is put in.
levels.2: Several tissue rolls stand fixed on the cardboard base, painted and patterned, and hold pencils upright.
levels.3: Trying a taller holder for rulers or scissors, extra rolls are added and the base is widened so it does not tip.

rows.name: Traditional Festival Craft (Fortnight 8)
steps: Make a rakhi or a wall hanging.
Decorate it using beads.
Discuss its cultural significance.
rows.materials: threads, beads, decorative paper

levels.0: No rakhi or wall hanging is finished, or the threads and beads stay loose.
levels.1: With a model rakhi on the table and a partner threading, beads are fixed but the design copies the model.
levels.2: A rakhi or wall hanging with threads and beads, tied firmly and decorated, is finished and held up.
levels.3: Explaining the cultural meaning of the rakhi to a classmate, a different festival item is also planned with its own beads.

rows.name: Collaborative Model Making (Fortnight 9)
steps: Divide the children into groups.
Plan a model.
Construct it together.
Present the final work.
rows.materials: mixed recycled materials, tape, glue, paint
rows.note: Observation focus: teamwork, planning, material handling, problem solving.

levels.0: No agreed plan appears before building starts, or the model has one maker while the others only watch.
levels.1: With the educator's role cards for planning, the group draws a plan and glues the recycled pieces into a model, though one member still needs a reminder to join the build.
levels.2: A drawn plan that every group member has agreed to becomes a finished model of mixed recycled materials held with tape and glue, and each member presents their own part.
levels.3: Faced with a new brief such as a bridge, the group sketches a fresh plan, swaps a failed material, and explains to the class which change fixed the wobble.

rows.name: Describe the Object – verbal game (June)
steps: Warm-up: show the picture or object and predict what it is.
One child describes an object using describing words (visheshan) without naming it.
The class guesses.
Use the same words in a spoken sentence.
rows.materials: objects or pictures

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – June: Describe the Object

rows.note: Doc names the project; steps follow its 5-step introduction system.

levels.0: Describing words are missing, or the object is simply named, so the class has nothing to guess from.
levels.1: Using a word bank of visheshan cards, the describer offers two describing words and the class still needs a third before guessing the object.
levels.2: Three or more visheshan such as लंबा, मीठा or गोल are spoken without naming the object, and the class guesses it correctly.
levels.3: Given a fresh picture, the describer speaks a full sentence with visheshan placed before the noun and explains why each word narrowed the guess.

rows.name: Tense-timeline storytelling (July)
steps: Draw a timeline with past, present and future.
Tell a short story that moves along the timeline.
Say which tense each part uses.
rows.materials: timeline strip

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – July: Tense-timeline storytelling

rows.note: Doc names the project; steps built from its grammar focus.

levels.0: Story stays in one tense throughout, or the timeline strip is left unlabelled with no tense named.
levels.1: Pointing to a timeline strip with past, present and future marked, the story shifts tense only when the educator reminds which section is next.
levels.2: A short story moves left to right along the timeline, and each part uses a verb form matching its past, present or future section, named aloud.
levels.3: Retelling a morning routine as yesterday and as tomorrow, the storyteller rewrites the same verbs in each tense and explains how the endings change.

rows.name: Sandhi split puzzle cards (August)
steps: Make puzzle cards with joined words and their parts.
Match each joined word to its split parts.
Check with a partner.
rows.materials: puzzle cards

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – August: Sandhi split puzzle cards

rows.note: Doc names the project.

levels.0: Puzzle cards stay unmatched, or joined words are paired with parts that do not make the word.
levels.1: Checking with a partner and an answer card, joined words are matched to their parts, with two or three cards fixed after the check.
levels.2: Each joined word card is matched to its correct split parts, such as विद्या + आलय for विद्यालय, and the partner confirms every pair.
levels.3: Handed unseen joined words, the pair splits them without the answer card and says which sounds merged at the joint.

rows.name: Anekarthi riddle cards (September)
steps: Write riddle cards for words with more than one meaning.
Read a riddle aloud; a partner gives the word.
Say both meanings of the word.
rows.materials: riddle cards

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – September: Anekarthi riddle cards

rows.note: Doc names the project.

levels.0: Riddle cards give only one meaning of the word, or the partner cannot name the word at all.
levels.1: With a picture clue beside each riddle card, the partner names the word and states both meanings after a nudge.
levels.2: A riddle card read aloud leads the partner to the word, and both of its meanings, such as कल for yesterday and tomorrow, are said.
levels.3: Writing a new riddle card for a different word, the writer gives two clues pointing to its two meanings and uses each in a sentence.

rows.name: Write a letter to a friend about a festival (October)
steps: See the informal letter format.
Write a letter to a friend about a festival.
Swap with a partner and check the format.
rows.materials: paper, pencils

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – October: letter to a friend about a festival

rows.note: Doc names the project.

levels.0: No letter is written, or the page describes a festival with no greeting, closing or sign-off.
levels.1: Copying from the displayed format sample, the letter has address, greeting and closing in place but only one brief line about the festival.
levels.2: A letter to a friend holds the date, a greeting, two or more lines about the festival, and a closing with the writer's name.
levels.3: Asked to reply as the friend, the writer produces a second letter in the same format answering with a festival of their own.

rows.name: Muhavare skit performance (November)
steps: Choose one of the 10 common idioms and proverbs.
Prepare a short skit that shows its meaning.
Perform it; the audience guesses the idiom.

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – November: Muhavare skit performance

rows.note: Doc names the project.

levels.0: No skit is prepared, or the performance does not show the idiom's meaning so the audience cannot guess it.
levels.1: With the idiom card and a meaning hint from the educator, the group acts a scene and the audience guesses only after a second showing.
levels.2: The performed skit shows the idiom's meaning through action and speech, and the audience names the muhavara on the first showing.
levels.3: Choosing a second idiom unseen in class, the group builds a skit in a new setting and explains both its literal and its intended meaning.

rows.name: Two-line dialogue role-play (December)
steps: Write a two-line dialogue between two people.
Role-play it with a partner.
Write it in the notebook for the writing sample.
rows.materials: notebook

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – December: two-line dialogue role-play

rows.note: Doc names the project.

levels.0: Only one speaker's line appears in the notebook, or no role-play takes place.
levels.1: Using a sentence-starter card, the two-line dialogue is written and read, with the partner supplying the reply line.
levels.2: Two lines in the notebook show two different speakers with correct dialogue marks, and the role-play with the partner matches the written lines.
levels.3: Extending the dialogue to a new setting such as a shop, the writer adds more turns and the role-play keeps each speaker distinct.

rows.name: Student-led Hindi vocabulary quiz for younger grades (January)
steps: Prepare quiz questions from the Hindi vocabulary bank.
Go to a younger class and run the quiz.
Say the answers and the meanings.
rows.materials: vocabulary bank

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – January: student-led vocabulary quiz

rows.note: Doc names the project.

levels.0: No quiz questions are prepared, or the visit ends without a single question reaching the younger class.
levels.1: Reading from a question sheet checked by the educator, the quiz is run, with prompts needed before the answers and meanings are said.
levels.2: Quiz questions drawn from the vocabulary bank are asked aloud to the younger class, and answers and meanings are given correctly.
levels.3: Meeting a wrong answer from a younger child, the quizmaster rephrases the question with a hint and explains the word's meaning in simple Hindi.

rows.name: Hindi Diwas showcase – writing wall display (February)
steps: Write a 7–8 line paragraph with an introduction, body and conclusion.
Display it on the writing wall.
Read the wall and say one thing you liked.
rows.materials: chart paper

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – February: Hindi Diwas showcase

rows.note: Doc names the project; Hindi Diwas is 14 September.

levels.0: No paragraph reaches the writing wall, or what is pinned up has only a line or two.
levels.1: With a frame of introduction, body and conclusion boxes, a 7-8 line paragraph is written and pinned up.
levels.2: A 7-8 line paragraph with a visible introduction, body and conclusion is displayed on the writing wall and read by classmates.
levels.3: Visiting the wall, the writer reads another paragraph, names one feature liked, and revises their own conclusion using it.

rows.name: Hindi Mela – Grade 4 hosts stalls (March)
steps: Plan a stall that shows a year of Hindi learning.
Host the stall and mentor younger children.
Explain the activity to each visitor.
rows.materials: stall materials

source.cell: Section 8 Grade 4 month-by-month plan – March: Hindi Mela

rows.note: Doc says Grade 4 hosts stalls and mentors younger grades.

levels.0: Visitors pass the stall without hearing any explanation, or the host stays silent.
levels.1: Holding a prepared card at the stall, the host explains the activity to a younger visitor while a partner fills the gaps.
levels.2: Each visiting younger child hears the stall's activity explained in clear spoken Hindi and then tries it with the host guiding.
levels.3: Answering an unexpected question from a visitor, the host rephrases the explanation and links the stall to something learned earlier in the year.

rows.name: Antakshari Fridays
steps: Play a 10-minute Hindi word-chain game to close the week.
Each word begins with the last letter of the previous word.
Continue around the class.
rows.note: Doc: 10-minute Hindi word-chain game.

levels.0: A word starts with a letter other than the previous word's last letter, or the chain breaks with no new word offered.
levels.1: With a letter chart on the board, the chain continues but takes a pause and a hint to find the next word.
levels.2: Round the class, each Hindi word begins with the last letter of the word before it, for ten minutes without a break in the chain.
levels.3: Given a tricky ending letter, the player offers a valid word and explains why it fits, or sets a theme such as animals for the next round.

rows.name: Hindi-Only Hour
steps: Choose one low-pressure hour each week.
Speak only Hindi, mistakes included.
Do not correct anyone mid-sentence.
rows.note: Doc: one hour weekly, no correction mid-sentence.

levels.0: English words fill most of the hour, or no full Hindi sentences are heard.
levels.1: With a word bank of common Hindi phrases on display, Hindi is spoken in short sentences and English slips in when a word is missing.
levels.2: Throughout the hour, sentences are spoken in Hindi only, and mistakes are left uncorrected while the speaker keeps going.
levels.3: Stuck on an unfamiliar word, the speaker describes it in other Hindi words rather than switching to English and keeps the talk going.

rows.name: Reading Buddies
steps: Pair a Grade 4 child with a younger child once a month.
Share a read-aloud together.
The older child reads the Hindi story aloud.
rows.materials: Hindi story book
rows.note: Doc: monthly shared read-aloud with younger grades.

levels.0: The story is not read aloud, or the younger partner hears only a few words of it.
levels.1: Following the finger along the page with the younger partner, the older child reads the story with help from the educator on hard words.
levels.2: A Hindi story book is read aloud in full to the younger buddy, in a clear voice with the pages turned together.
levels.3: Stopping mid-story, the reader asks the younger partner what happens next and explains a new word on the page.

rows.name: Word Wall
steps: After every chapter add new words to the class wall.
Write each word with its meaning.
Read the wall at the start of the next period.
rows.materials: wall space, cards
rows.note: Doc: a growing, student-built wall.

levels.0: No new card reaches the wall, or a card shows a word with no meaning beside it.
levels.1: Taking words from the chapter's list, a card is added with the meaning filled in with the educator's help.
levels.2: After the chapter, a card showing a new Hindi word and its written meaning is added to the wall and read at the next period.
levels.3: Choosing a word nobody else added, the child uses it in a sentence on the card and explains how it differs from a similar word.

rows.name: Comic Strip Making (Grades 3–4)
steps: Choose a chapter story.
Turn it into a 4-panel comic strip.
Share the strip with a partner.
rows.materials: paper, colours
rows.note: Doc: turn a chapter's story into a 4-panel comic strip.

levels.0: Fewer than four panels are drawn, or the panels do not follow the chapter story.
levels.1: Using a four-box template with the story's four key events listed, the panels are filled and the partner helps put them in order.
levels.2: Four panels in sequence show the chapter story's events, each with a picture and a short Hindi caption, and the strip is shared with a partner.
levels.3: Switching to a different chapter, the strip keeps four panels with a clear beginning and ending, and the partner can retell the story from the strip alone.

rows.name: Warehouse and packing: division with remainders
steps: Place-value distribution of real quantities, such as a warehouse of items to pack.
Use area models and number lines.
Break large numbers into friendly chunks.
Pack items into boxes and talk about the remainder.
rows.materials: real quantities, packing objects

source.cell: Division master summary – Grade 4 row (Warehouse, packing, remainder problems)

rows.note: Doc names the Grade 4 games and models; steps follow its Grade 4 row.

levels.0: Items are counted out but never grouped into boxes, or no remainder is named.
levels.1: With a number line printed on the sheet and counters, groups of the box size are taken out and the remainder is counted after a nudge.
levels.2: A warehouse total is packed into boxes of equal size by grouping or jumping back on a number line, and the leftover items are named as the remainder.
levels.3: Given a new packing problem such as 87 books in boxes of 6, the packer predicts the number of full boxes and explains what the remainder means there.

rows.name: Data Detective: reading large numbers in real data
steps: Use real-world large numbers (data).
Use charts and number lines to read them.
Reason about number size and construct numbers.
Play estimation challenges.
rows.materials: data cards, place-value charts

source.cell: Place value + comparison master summary – Grade 4 row (Data detective, estimation challenges)

rows.note: Doc names the Grade 4 games; steps follow its Grade 4 row.

levels.0: Large numbers on the data cards are read as digit strings, with no place-value breakdown shown.
levels.1: Placing digits on a place-value chart, the number is split into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones with the chart doing most of the work.
levels.2: A real data number such as 4,735 is written as 4 thousands, 7 hundreds, 3 tens and 5 ones without the chart.
levels.3: Building a number to fit an estimation challenge, the player shows its parts and explains which place decides whether it is bigger than another number.

rows.name: Weekly Math Challenge – Monday problem
steps: Solve the problem on the Monday sheet using the working space.
Write the final answer.
Review the answers by the end of the week.
Join the quick review session of the most challenging problems.
rows.materials: WeekMath Challenge sheet

source.cell: Challenge list (34 topics) and Monday sheet

rows.note: Doc lists 34 weekly topics, from 2-digit addition word problems to mixed revision; planner says Friday, doc says Monday.

levels.0: The Monday sheet is returned blank, or the working space holds no attempt at the problem.
levels.1: Using the working space and a reminder of the steps, an answer is written but needs the review session to be corrected.
levels.2: Working in the space on the Monday sheet leads to a correct final answer that is written clearly.
levels.3: At the weekly review, a solved problem is re-explained aloud and then solved by a different method on a new number.

rows.name: Mind Game: weekly brain teaser
steps: Read the week's puzzle (for example spot the difference, odd one out, code breaker, tangram, logic grid, riddle).
Write your answer.
Write how you solved it.
rows.materials: Mind Game sheet
rows.note: Doc lists 34 challenge types; whether this is the "Think Outside the Box" slot is assumed.

levels.0: No answer is written on the Mind Game sheet, or the line on how it was solved is empty.
levels.1: With a hint from the educator or a partner, the puzzle's answer is written and the solving line is only a few words.
levels.2: The week's puzzle, such as an odd-one-out, has a correct answer written and a line saying how it was solved.
levels.3: Given a different puzzle type, such as a code breaker, the solver finds the answer and explains how the method from the earlier puzzle applied.
